title: The 50/30/20 Rule Explained, with Real Examples

excerpt: How the 50/30/20 budget works, what counts as a need or a want, and what to do when the numbers don't fit.
description: How the 50/30/20 budget rule works, what counts as needs, wants and savings, worked examples, and what to do when your rent takes more than half.
body:
The 50/30/20 rule is one of the simplest ways to budget. You split your take-home pay into three parts: about 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and paying off debt. It was popularised by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi in their 2005 book All Your Worth.

## The three parts

- **Needs, 50%.** Things you must pay to live and work: rent or mortgage, energy and water bills, council tax, food shopping, transport to work, insurance and the minimum payments on any debts.
- **Wants, 30%.** Things that make life better but you could live without: eating out, takeaways, streaming and other subscriptions, hobbies, new clothes beyond the basics and holidays.
- **Savings and debt, 20%.** An emergency fund, saving for goals, pension top-ups, and any extra payments that clear debt faster than the minimum.

## A worked example

Say your take-home pay is £2,500 a month, after tax.

- Needs: 50% is £1,250
- Wants: 30% is £750
- Savings and debt: 20% is £500

Over a year, that's £6,000 going to savings or clearing debt. Try your own numbers in the free [50/30/20 budget calculator](/tools/budget-calculator/).

## Always use take-home pay

The rule works on what actually reaches your account each month, after tax, National Insurance, pension contributions taken at source and any other deductions. Using your salary before tax makes every number too high.

## What if my needs are more than 50%?

That's very common, especially where rent is high. You have a few options:

- **Change the split.** 60/20/20 or 70/20/10 still keeps money going to savings every month. The calculator lets you switch between them.
- **Bring needs down over time.** Compare energy, phone and insurance deals when they renew.
- **Trim the wants first.** Subscriptions are an easy place to start. The [subscription calculator](/tools/subscription-calculator/) shows what they really cost over a year.

## Need or want? Some tricky ones

- **Phone contract:** the basic plan is a need, the upgrade is a want
- **Food:** the weekly shop is a need, takeaways are a want
- **Debt:** minimum payments are a need, overpayments go in the 20%
- **Gym:** usually a want, unless a cheaper option would do the same job

## Making it stick

- Track one month of spending first so you know your real numbers
- Move your savings on payday, before you start spending
- Build an emergency fund before saving for other goals
- Clearing debt? The [debt payoff calculator](/tools/debt-payoff-calculator/) shows the fastest way

The BudgetWise app has a built-in 50/30/20 planner and expense tracker, and never asks you to link a bank account.
